title: The Night the Library Whispered
blurb: Strange whispers drift through the town library after dark. Ama and her cousin decide to find the ghost.

chapters.title: Whispers After Dark
chapters.text:
The old library in Accra was Ama's favourite place. It smelled of paper and polish, the ceiling fans turned slowly overhead, and Mrs Boateng the librarian knew every book by heart. Ama came every afternoon to read, and she always chose the chair by the tall window.

On Tuesday, Mrs Boateng looked pale. "Something strange is happening," she whispered. "When I lock up at night and come back in the morning, I find books on the floor. They always come from the top shelves. And last night, the caretaker heard a voice in the empty reading room."

Ama stopped with her bag half off her shoulder. "What did the voice say?" she asked.

Mrs Boateng bent closer. "Shh, quiet please," she said.

"Sorry," whispered Ama. "But what did it say?"

"No, my dear. That is exactly what it said."

Ama's cousin Kwesi, who was sitting on the floor nearby, dropped his comic. Kwesi believed in everything: aliens, giant snails, and the story that the school cook could see through walls. "A library ghost!" he cried. Several people looked up. "A ghost who wants everyone to be quiet!"

Ama looked up too, at the shadowy top shelves. They were so high that Mrs Boateng needed a ladder to reach them. Why were the fallen books always from up there? Who could reach them in the dark, without a ladder?

She felt a question begin to itch inside her, the way it did at the start of a good mystery story.

"Or it could be a mystery," she said, and she grinned. "Tonight, we are going to find out."

She has knocked over Kwesi's comic by mistake

The shelves are too high for anyone to reach without a ladder
The caretaker has been reading them late at night

questions.why: She notices that Mrs Boateng needs a ladder for those shelves, and she asks who could reach them in the dark without one.

chapters.title: The Stake-Out
chapters.text:
That evening, Ama and Kwesi had a sleepover at Mrs Boateng's house, next door to the library. Their parents agreed at once, because Mrs Boateng was an old friend of the family. After a supper of jollof rice, she took a big iron key from a hook and held it out.

"Be careful," she said, "and do not touch anything. I will sit at my window, just across the yard. If you get frightened, flash your torch three times and I will come."

At ten o'clock, the cousins tiptoed into the dark reading room. The room they knew so well looked different at night. The chairs had long shadows, and the globe in the corner looked like a huge bald head. They hid behind a big sofa with a torch, a notebook and a packet of biscuits. Ama wrote the time at the top of a clean page.

The library was very still. The clock ticked. A tap dripped. Half an hour went by, and Ama's left leg went to sleep. Then Kwesi's stomach growled loudly.

"Shh!" said Ama.

"You sound just like the ghost," whispered Kwesi, and they both had to bite their sleeves to stop themselves laughing.

After a while, he stopped smiling. "What if it really is a ghost? What will we do?"

"We will ask it what it wants," whispered Ama. "Then we will write it down." She sounded braver than she felt.

Suddenly something rustled high above them. Both children froze. A little dust floated down through the moonlight from the window. Then came a soft, scratchy sound, like someone clearing a throat.

Under the sofa

chapters.title: Feathers
chapters.text:
Ama slowly raised her torch. Her hand was not quite steady. The beam travelled up the tall shelves, past the atlases and the dictionaries, to the very top. There, between two dusty encyclopaedias, sat a pair of round, shining eyes.

The eyes blinked.

"A ghost?" whispered Kwesi, hiding his face behind a cushion. "Does it have a face? Tell me if it has no face."

"Look," said Ama, and she began to laugh. "It has feathers."

Kwesi peeped out, one eye at a time. It was a large grey parrot with a bright red tail. It walked sideways along the shelf, and its claws went tick, tick, tick on the wood. Then it leaned on a thick book with its shoulder, just to see what would happen. The book slid to the edge, tipped over and fell. Thump. A puff of dust rose from the floor.

The parrot looked down and seemed very pleased.

Ama opened her notebook and wrote: Books on the floor. Explained.

The parrot looked at her and tilted its head. Then it opened its curved beak and said in a perfect, stern voice, "Shh! Quiet please!"

It was Mrs Boateng's voice exactly, with the same little sniff at the end.

The cousins burst out laughing. They laughed so hard that they had to hold on to each other, and Kwesi slid right off the sofa. "Our ghost," he gasped, "is a bird!"

Ama wiped her eyes. Then she stopped laughing and looked up again. "But whose bird?" she said. "And how did it get in?"

chapters.title: The Professor
chapters.text:
Ama flashed her torch three times at the window. Then she made a gentle clucking sound and held out a biscuit. The parrot looked at it with one eye. It looked again with the other eye. Then it hopped down the shelves, one step at a time, and took the biscuit from her fingers.

"He must be someone's pet," said Ama. "A wild bird would not do that." Around his leg was a thin metal ring. On it was a tiny label: Professor, 14 Mango Street.

The door creaked, and Mrs Boateng came in with a lamp. She stared at the parrot. The parrot stared at her. "Shh! Quiet please!" it said.

Her mouth fell open. "Do I really sound like that?"

"Exactly," said Kwesi.

She read the label and gave a small cry. "Mr Darko lives on Mango Street! He has a pet parrot, and last week it escaped through a window. He asked me to put up a notice about it." She turned to the board by the door, and there it was, in her own neat writing. "It has been up for a whole week, in the same room as the bird!"

"Poor Professor," said Ama. She worked it out aloud. "He must have flown in through that little high window, the one that you leave open for the air. It is quiet and warm here, and he has been listening to you every day. That is why he sounds just like you."

"But why push the books?" asked Mrs Boateng.

Kwesi shrugged. "He is bored. I would push books too, if I lived on a shelf."

The parrot sat on Ama's shoulder and began to eat his biscuit, dropping crumbs down her neck.

Parrots can only copy the voices of librarians

chapters.title: Case Closed
chapters.text:
The next morning, Ama and Kwesi carried Professor to Mr Darko's house. He rode on Ama's shoulder and said "Shh!" to a goat, two taxis and a woman selling oranges.

An empty cage hung on Mr Darko's porch with its little door wide open. Under it was a saucer of fresh seeds. The old man came out, saw the parrot and gasped. Then he cried happy tears. "My Professor! I looked for you everywhere!"

The parrot flapped his wings and said, "Hello, hello! Shh, quiet please!" Everyone laughed, though Mr Darko looked puzzled. "Where did he learn that?" he asked. "He only ever said hello."

"At the library," said Ama. "He has been studying."

Mr Darko thanked the children and promised to bring Mrs Boateng a basket of mangoes. Then he looked at the ring on the parrot's leg. "I will add my phone number to this label," he said, "in case he ever flies away again."

That afternoon, the library was calm. All the books stayed on their shelves. Mrs Boateng whispered a thank you to Ama and Kwesi and took down her notice. Then she looked around the silent room and sighed. "It is rather too quiet now," she said.

"Shh, quiet please," said Kwesi in a stern voice, with a little sniff at the end. Mrs Boateng laughed so loudly that everyone looked up.

High on the shelf, one small feather was left behind. Ama climbed the ladder and brought it down as a souvenir. She pressed it into her notebook, and under it she wrote: The Library Ghost. Case closed.

questions.prompt: Who did Professor say "Shh!" to on the way to Mr Darko's house?
options: A hen, two teachers and a boy eating rice
A goat, two taxis and a woman selling oranges
A dog, two buses and a man selling mangoes
A cat, two bicycles and a child with a kite
questions.why: He rode on Ama's shoulder and said "Shh!" to a goat, two taxis and a woman selling oranges.

questions.prompt: What do the open cage and fresh seeds suggest about Mr Darko?
options: He was still hoping that his parrot would come home
He was tired of looking after a noisy parrot
He was keeping the seeds for wild birds
He had decided to get a new and different pet
questions.why: The cage door was left open, and the seeds were fresh. Together with his words, "I looked for you everywhere", they show that he had not given up.

questions.prompt: What did Professor use to say before he went to the library?
options: Only his own name
Only quiet please
Only hello
Only goodbye
questions.why: Mr Darko says, "He only ever said hello."

questions.prompt: What did Mr Darko promise to give Mrs Boateng?
options: A young parrot
A large cake
A box of books
A basket of mangoes
questions.why: He promised to bring Mrs Boateng a basket of mangoes.

questions.prompt: Why will Mr Darko add his phone number to the label?
options: So that Mrs Boateng can phone him about mangoes
So that Professor can learn to say the number
So that anyone who finds Professor can call him
So that the library can send him more notices
questions.why: He says he will add it "in case he ever flies away again". A finder could then call him at once.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs Boateng mean by "It is rather too quiet now"?
options: She is worried that another ghost has arrived
She misses the fuss that Professor caused
She wants people to start talking in the library
She thinks the ceiling fans have stopped working
questions.why: She looks around the silent room and sighs, and then she laughs when Kwesi copies the parrot. So she misses the excitement a little.

questions.prompt: What did Ama keep as a souvenir?
options: A small feather
The metal ring
The notice from the board
A half-eaten biscuit
questions.why: One small feather was left behind, and Ama brought it down as a souvenir.
